title: Consolidation case: recover and publish one corrected partner feed
goal: Join file identity, deterministic MERGE, repair, compute scaling, and live sharing into one safe release decision.
concept:
A carrier sends shipments.csv. At 09:00 it contains 100 orders. At 09:10 the carrier replaces the same path with a corrected file. The new batch has two rows for order 42. Validation then fails after writing 60 rows. Ten analysts are waiting, and a partner reads a live share.

This is not five separate problems. It is one release decision. A safe path must identify the corrected file, choose one winner for order 42, repair without duplicating rows, match compute to the workload, and expose only a certified view.
example: The release has five gates. Identity: treat the corrected object as a new version, not “the same filename.” Winner: rank order 42 by event_time and a stable tie-breaker before MERGE. Repair: restart the failed branch with repeat-safe writes. Capacity: one heavy reconciliation query needs more per-query power; many waiting readers need concurrency. Share: add or keep the certified view only after reconciliation passes; revoke access if bad data escaped.

use_case.when: Use this runbook when a file-fed pipeline must recover from corrected inputs and publish current data to internal or external consumers.
use_case.example: A logistics partner overwrites shipments.csv, duplicate business keys appear, validation partially writes, and a partner share is already live.
use_case.decision: Stop publication first. Prove input identity and one-row-per-key determinism, repair with idempotent writes, choose compute from queue/profile evidence, then expose the narrow certified object. Treat every gate as evidence, not a checkbox.

practice: Toggle each control. The release board names the first unsafe gate and shows which data may reach the partner.
boundary: The browser is a local decision model, not Databricks or Snowflake. It uses five binary gates and ignores storage consistency, transactions across systems, schema drift, masking, cross-region replication, costs, and real query plans. Vendor SQL is illustrative and unexecuted.

function paintRelease(){const gates=[['identity',identityOk.checked],['winner',winnerOk.checked],['repair',repairOk.checked],['capacity',capacityOk.checked],['share',shareOk.checked]],bad=gates.find(x=>!x[1]);releaseWorld.innerHTML='
'+gates.map(([n,ok])=>'
'+n+'
'+(ok?'evidence passes':'STOP here')+'
').join('')+'

'+(bad?'DO NOT PUBLISH · first failed gate: '+bad[0]:'PUBLISH CERTIFIED VIEW · all five gates pass')+'

';};[identityOk,winnerOk,repairOk,capacityOk,shareOk].forEach(x=>x.onchange=paintRelease);paintRelease();
questions: The partner overwrites the same path. What identity should drive reprocessing?
Filename alone
A version/content identity plus audit metadata
Order count only
A stable path can point at changed bytes; preserve version/content evidence.
Two staged rows match order 42. What happens before MERGE?

Let the engine pick
Insert both
One deterministic source winner removes ambiguous updates.
Reconciliation fails after a partial write. What may be shared?
The raw target immediately
Only the last certified view; stop or revoke the bad publication path
Every repair attempt
Publication is a correctness boundary, not merely the last task.

steps.note: Represent the five pieces of release evidence.
The corrected object keeps its stable path but gains a new version identity.
A total order selects the same winner on every retry.

steps.code: release='PUBLISH' if all(gates.values()) and winner['seq']==2 else 'STOP'
steps.note: Publication occurs only when every gate has evidence.

title: The urgent thread waits while ordinary work runs
goal: See priority inversion and how priority inheritance lets the lock owner finish.
concept:
A paramedic needs a medicine cabinet. A cleaner has the key, but an ordinary delivery keeps interrupting the cleaner. The paramedic waits even though the delivery is less urgent.

In software, a low-priority thread holds a lock needed by a high-priority thread. Medium-priority work keeps preempting the lock owner. This is priority inversion. With priority inheritance, the lock owner temporarily inherits the waiter’s higher priority so it can finish and release the lock.
example: Low L holds the Kafka checkpoint lock for two ticks. High H arrives and blocks. Medium M becomes runnable. Without inheritance, M runs before L, so H waits longer. With inheritance, L is boosted above M, runs its remaining two ticks, unlocks, and H proceeds.

use_case.when: Use priority-inheritance synchronization when bounded latency matters and a high-priority thread may wait on a lock held by lower-priority work.
use_case.example: A real-time ingestion controller waits for a checkpoint mutex while a background metrics thread owns it and normal compression work is runnable.
use_case.decision: First shorten critical sections and avoid unnecessary shared locks. When real-time scheduling is truly required, use an owner-aware PI mutex supported by the OS/runtime; a counting semaphore has no single owner to boost.

practice: Switch priority inheritance on and off. Follow who owns the lock and which thread the scheduler runs at each tick.
boundary: This deterministic toy has three threads, one lock, fixed work, and no interrupts or nested lock chains. Actual schedulers, runtime safepoints, I/O, cgroups, and non-preemptible regions change latency. Priority inheritance bounds one inversion mechanism; it does not guarantee every deadline.

title: Stop starting six migrations; finish two
goal: Use a portfolio work-in-progress limit to turn scattered effort into completed evidence.
concept:
Six half-built bridges do not move any traffic. A platform portfolio can look busy the same way: six migrations are “in progress,” but every team waits for reviews, security decisions, or scarce platform engineers.

A work-in-progress (WIP) limit caps how many initiatives may actively consume the constrained team. New work waits until one item is finished or explicitly stopped. The purpose is flow and learning—not keeping people idle.
example: Two platform engineers can complete two small migrations every two weeks. Starting six at once spreads attention across all six; after two weeks, each is roughly one-third complete and no decommission evidence exists. With WIP=2, two finish, produce cost and risk evidence, then the next two start.

use_case.when: Use a portfolio WIP limit when many “priority” migrations compete for the same reviewers, platform team, or release windows and completion dates keep slipping.
use_case.example: Six Kafka-to-managed-stream migrations share two platform specialists and one security review lane.
use_case.decision: Find the real constraint, set a visible limit at that point, define “done,” and force an explicit start/stop choice. Do not hide urgent incidents or make the number a productivity target.

practice: Choose the WIP limit. The board shows completed migrations after two timeboxes and how many remain merely started.
boundary: This arithmetic model assumes equal-sized work, one bottleneck, no blocked dependencies, and two units of capacity per timebox. Real portfolios need item slicing, variability, expedite policies, and outcome measures. A WIP limit reveals tradeoffs; it does not choose strategy for you.

title: Approve this exact tool call—not every future call
goal: Bind human approval to the inspected call and revalidate immediately before execution.
tag: Harness engineering · human in the loop
concept:
A manager signs a purchase order for 10 laptops. That signature should not authorize a later order for 100 servers just because both use the “buy” system.

An agent approval should name the tool call the person inspected: tool, parsed arguments, call identity, and relevant policy context. Resume the same paused run state. Before execution, re-run input guardrails because conditions may have changed while the human was deciding.
example: The agent proposes cancelOrder({orderId:42}). The UI displays order 42 and stores approval for call call_A. A later proposal cancelOrder({orderId:99}) has call call_B. It needs a new decision. A sticky “always approve this tool” choice is broader and should be rare, explicit, and policy-bounded.

use_case.when: Use call-specific approval for tools that spend money, delete data, change access, message people, or otherwise create hard-to-reverse effects.
use_case.example: A support agent may cancel one customer order after a human reviews the exact order ID and reason.
use_case.decision: Render parsed arguments and impact, approve/reject the pending item on the same run state, then revalidate authorization and policy just before execution. Avoid sticky approval for arguments whose risk varies.

practice: Approve call A, then change the proposed order. The receipt stays bound to A and the new call remains blocked.
boundary: The browser uses a simple call-ID and argument fingerprint. It does not run the OpenAI Agents SDK, authenticate the reviewer, protect serialized state, prevent UI spoofing, or solve concurrent state changes. Cryptographic hashing alone does not establish authorization; execution-side checks remain required.

title: Fan out light, apply weights in place, read many sums at once
goal: Understand the FAST-ONN research mechanism without treating a lab benchmark as a shipped processor.
concept:
Imagine projecting one stencil onto many tiles at once instead of carrying each tile to one calculator. FAST-ONN fans out light from a dense laser array. A spatial light modulator stores many weights in the optical path. Detectors read many weighted sums in parallel.

“In-memory” here means weights are applied where the optical signal travels, reducing repeated movement between a separate weight store and arithmetic unit. Differential readout represents signed weights with paired positive and negative channels.
example: A tiny teaching kernel has four inputs [1,0,1,1] and weights [+1,-1,+1,0]. The optical paths contribute [1,0,1,0]; the detector sum is 2. The paper reports a 5×5 VCSEL array and 3×3 parallel kernels at 100 mega-subimages/s, corresponding to 0.9 billion convolutions/s in its experiment.

use_case.when: Use this concept when evaluating research hardware for extremely high-throughput, low-latency convolution near sensors.
use_case.example: An edge vision system must extract simple features from a very fast optical stream before sending a smaller representation onward.
use_case.decision: Ask whether the demonstrated workload, accuracy, reprogramming, calibration, precision, size, power accounting, and system I/O match the intended product. Treat the published device as research evidence, not a drop-in GPU replacement.

practice: Change one input bit. The parallel path contributions and detector sum update together.
boundary: This exact integer dot product is a teaching model, not a simulation of diffraction, VCSEL noise, signed differential circuits, calibration, nonlinear layers, training, energy, or throughput. The paper’s 2026 benchmark is a specific experimental system and does not establish general production superiority.

title: A skipped required workflow can wait forever
goal: Keep the required check present even when expensive jobs are irrelevant to the changed paths.
concept:
A building guard expects a stamped form. If the form office stays closed because your delivery is “documents only,” the guard does not interpret that as approval. The stamp never arrives.

GitHub behaves similarly: if path filtering skips an entire required workflow, its associated check can remain Pending and block the pull request. A skipped job, by contrast, reports Success. Keep a stable required gate job present on every relevant pull request and conditionally skip only the expensive work.
example: ci is required. A docs-only pull request does not match paths: src/**, so the entire workflow never runs and ci waits. Fix the shape: trigger the workflow for every pull request, detect changed paths inside it, run build only when needed, and have a small final required-gate job report success when work is irrelevant or verify all needed jobs when relevant.

use_case.when: Use this pattern when branch rules require a GitHub Actions check but some file changes do not need the expensive test/deploy jobs.
use_case.example: Documentation-only changes should skip a 20-minute integration suite without leaving the required CI check pending.
use_case.decision: Keep the required check name and workflow trigger stable. Put conditional logic at job/step level, and test docs-only, code-only, mixed, and merge-queue events.

practice: Switch between workflow-level path filtering and an always-triggered gate. The PR check changes from Pending to Success.
boundary: The browser models one required check and two change types. Real rulesets match exact check names and apps, path filters have diff limits, merge queues require merge_group, and needs/always() semantics matter. Test the actual repository rules and event payloads.

title: gRPC retries stop when response headers commit the RPC
goal: Place retryable failures before the commit point and make side effects safe.
concept:
A courier can try another route while the sealed delivery receipt is still blank. Once the recipient signs, the courier stops choosing routes and hands the outcome to you.

gRPC can buffer a call’s history and create a new attempt after eligible failures. But once the client receives response headers, the RPC is committed: gRPC stops automatic retry and gives control to the application.
example: Attempt 1 sends Reserve(order-42). If the transport closes with configured UNAVAILABLE before response headers, a policy may start attempt 2 after backoff. If headers arrive and the stream later fails, there is no automatic retry. The application must interpret the outcome. Because a server may have performed work before a failure is observed, use an idempotency key for side effects.

use_case.when: Use configured gRPC retries for transient failures on calls whose replay risk is understood and bounded.
use_case.example: A reservation RPC briefly hits an unavailable replica before any response headers are returned.
use_case.decision: Set a realistic deadline, retry only appropriate status codes with bounded attempts/backoff, throttle retry storms, and use idempotency keys or read-only semantics. Do not retry FAILED_PRECONDITION until state is fixed.

practice: Move the failure before or after response headers. The attempt timeline shows whether gRPC may retry automatically.
boundary: This browser ignores language-specific support, service-config delivery, pushback, throttling, jitter, hedging, streaming details, deadlines, and server-side execution races. It does not contact a gRPC server. Retry safety depends on method semantics and idempotency beyond the client library.
